newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli peacemaker sparks row over meeting Peres.
newsitem.headline: Israeli peacemaker sparks row over meeting Peres.

text.p: An Israeli general conducting peace talks with the Palestinians drew political fire on Thursday after a newspaper published a front-page photo showing him leaving the home of opposition leader Shimon Peres.
The Maariv newspaper said Major-General Oren Shahor met Peres three times in the last two months and also former Labour cabinet minister Yossi Beilin.

Right-wingers quickly took aim at the general, engaged in protracted talks with the PLO on behalf of the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on civilian issues linked to an Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron.

"If the point of these meetings is passing secret information without prior authorisation, without the knowledge of the defence minister, it's prohibited," said Uzi Landau, a top parliament member from the ruling Likud party.
Shahor was photographed, in uniform, outside Peres's home on Wednesday. The officer had been a peace negotiator under Peres, Israel's prime minister until Netanyahu ousted him in elections in May.
"The prime minister didn't know about the meeting of General Shahor with Peres. A response will be provided later," Netanyahu's office told Reuters.

A spokesman for Shahor confirmed the meetings but said the general had not asked for official permission since they were merely social calls and had no connection to the negotiations with the Palestinians.
The affair underscored the traditionally close relations between Israel's political leaders and its generals.

Political parties have actively courted top officers before their retirement from the service, and many have gone on to hold key cabinet posts. Israel's top soldier in the 1967 Middle East war, Yitzhak Rabin, was twice prime minister.
Former army chief, cabinet minister Rafael Eitan, said Shahor should no longer remain in the regular army.
"He should be walking around with a reservist card," Eitan said.
"Only in a fascist country could such a headline top a newspaper," he told army radio.
